The first half in Istanbul is brought to an end and we are all square heading into the break. Liverpool took the lead through Nyoni but Greenwood’s deflected free-kick has Fenerbahce on level terms at half-time.

One added minute at the end of this first half.

Greenwood has been Fenerbahce’s best player by far tonight and he tests Alisson. Lukaku finds Greenwood with a pass forward down the left channel and, from inside the Liverpool penalty area, the latter forces Alisson into a decent save.

What started off as an encouraging performance has descended into something ordinary at best for Liverpool. They are being overrun in midfield and the pace of Greenwood down Fenerbahce’s right has the beating of Kostas Tsimikas on every occasion. Andoni Iraola will be delighted to get in for half-time all square - if Liverpool can see it out.

Greenwood has an opportunity from the right side of the box. He tries to beat Alisson at his near post but drags it wide.

Munoz’s cross from near the byline is met by Barcola and the Frenchman’s header goes narrowly wide of the far post.

Tsimikas’ inswinging corner from the right is put into a dangerous area and Skriniar’s header goes over his own bar for another on the other side. Szoboszlai feeds one in towards the near post and Lukaku heads away.

Mason Greenwood is having his name bellowed around the stadium though the deflection off Jeremy Jacquet is the only reason he has scored. Emotions are running high in the stadium, especially in the press box which seems to be an overspill for home supporters. One of Trey Nyoni’s former coaches has an observer’s seat here and he cheered why Nyoni scored. Greenwood’s leveller saw those who had taken umbrage at something so inoffensive return the cheering ten-fold with some pretty colourful gestures, too.

The hosts are back on level terms. Fenerbahce have a free-kick not far outside the Liverpool penalty area, one that should never have been given after Szoboszlai is penalised for a foul on Kante that was not a foul. Greenwood steps up to take and his free-kick takes a huge deflection off Jacquet. That deflection takes it away from Alisson and into the Liverpool net. Alisson is not impressed with his wall.

Fenerbahce are inches away from equalising moments after going behind as they hit the frame of the goal. Brown’s cross from the left side of the box finds Kahveci, whose shot comes back off the bar. It would have been a very close call with offside had the ball gone in.

The visitors take the lead in Istanbul and it is 19-year-old Nyoni who scores. A cross from Szoboszlai into the Fenerbahce penalty area is headed out to the edge of the box, where Nyoni volleys it first time. The shot takes a small deflection off Oppong and beats Ederson.

What a moment for Trey Nyoni 🥹 The young Liverpool midfielder scores his first professional goal, and he does it on the Champions League stage ✨ 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Vtj4Yd3tnn

Fenerbahce want a penalty. The ball is played in behind the Liverpool defence and Greenwood takes a sensational first touch. Tsimikas races back and there is a small push on Greenwood, who goes down. The referee waves the appeals away and the VAR clears the incident.

Should Barcola have done better there? Ngumoha finds Gomez in acres of space out on the right. Gomez then first time delivers a very dangerous cross right through the corridor of uncertainty looking for Barcola but the Frenchman cannot connect.

Munoz wins Liverpool a corner out on the right after Yuksek blocked the cross from the Spaniard. Szoboszlai’s outswinger is headed away at the near post by Yuksek, who has made two good defensive actions in a matter of moments.

Liverpool have so much more quality on the ball when they keep possession but the final ball - especially from the left hand side - is letting them down at the moment. They are making light of a sodden pitch and some overzealous attempts by Fenerbahce to disrupt them. The first 15 minutes has been played out primarily to a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling but, looking at those fans around us, none of them are getting involved. Could it be the whistles are being piped in on a pre-recorded file?

Szoboszlai hits the free-kick but ends up hitting his own man. The effort did appear to be going on target but Munoz got in the way. Liverpool’s plan to set up a mini wall of their own to block out the view of Ederson backfired.

Ngumoha shows great footwork to skip past a few Fenerbahce defenders before Kante barges right into the back of the English teenager to give Liverpool a free-kick not far outside the Fenerbahce penalty area.

Liverpool have dominated possession in these early stages and have settled into the game well. Fenerbahce may not be in the best of form but this is still a tricky away trip.

Liverpool come close to the opening goal of the game. Tsimikas’ cross from the left comes all the way to the back post, where Munoz hits it. The Spaniard scuffs his effort and the ball comes to Barcola, who also scuffs his shot. The ball comes back to Munoz, whose powerful shot is parried behind by Ederson for a corner.

Fenerbahce deal with the initial delivery but Liverpool keep it alive. Szoboszlai sends in a dangerous delivery, which Jacquet meets, but the Frenchman’s header from six yards out goes wide. Jacquet should have done better with that chance.

Before we get going, we pause to pay tribute to Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died the other day.

We are under way in Istanbul, with the weather similar tonight in Turkey as to what it was like in Barcelona last night. Can Liverpool make it four wins from four in this season’s Champions League?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel into the pouring rain and we are moments away from kick-off in Istanbul. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Fenerbahce: Ederson; Semedo, Skriniar, Oppong, Brown; Guendouzi, Kante, Yuksek; Greenwood, Lukaku, Kahveci. Substitutes: Cetin, Akurktoglu, Demir, Muldur, Muriqi, Mercan, Elmaz, Nene, Aydin, Mimovic.

Liverpool: Alisson; Gomez, Jacquet, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; Szoboszlai, Mac Allister, Nyoni, Munoz, Barcola, Ngumoha.Substitutes: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Kerkez, Wirtz, Isak, Gakpo, Araujo, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Koumas.

A remarkable little stat for you to digest before kick-off. So many of Fenerbahce’s team were Premier League regulars, which begged the question - is this a team with more English top-flight experience than Liverpool? The answer is here: Liverpool’s starting line-up has 1241 Premier League appearances. Fenerbahce have 1086.

“I think we have been [rotating] basically all the season. You play every three, four days you have to refresh the legs. The defensive positions we do not have as many options. We have injuries but offensively I think we can rotate a little bit and today we can see other players.”

On Bradley Barcola playing as a central striker:

“I think Bradley, even Victor [Munoz], are players that are wingers but have played sometimes up front. I think we should be mobile. I think we should attack the spaces that are there. They are there to have good combinations outside. We do not expect them to stay there as the nine. I think Bradley can do this job very well.”

The Hungarian has been struggling of late with a hamstring injury but, having returned to the matchday squad on Sunday against Arsenal, he is now back into the starting XI tonight.

Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool’s head coach explained in the heat of the moment that he would tell his players to go down if they felt contact in the area and Cody Gakpo, the Netherlands international, explained last night in Istanbul it was a message the squad had taken on board.

“As a team, we play pretty fair – maybe we should dive some more like the gaffer said,” Gakpo, who also had claims to be awarded a penalty against Arsenal, explained. “On both occasions you could have given a penalty or a foul, but they decided not. We have to live with the decision. That’s it.”

But as angry as he was with the situation, Iraola has drawn a line on the matter. He is not going to seek out Pro Ref for a discussion – even though he feels a number of decisions have gone against Liverpool this season – and is channelling his energy into other situations.

Iraola said: “I didn’t ask for an explanation and I haven’t received an explanation, no. I told you what you I think about the plays but, honestly, I don’t have the time to [speak to Pro Ref]. I have been preparing for Fenerbahce. It is just two days between games so I have just been focusing on this game and the opposition and how to prepare the team.”

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

The Danish legend missed out on his country's only major tournament victory

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 30 years on, Denmark's Euro 92 victory remains one of international football's most remarkable stories.

A team that had failed to qualify for the tournament would eventually go on to lift the trophy, having taken full advantage of Yugoslavia's ejection following the break-up of the country.

Goals from John Jensen and Kim Vilfort sealed a 2-0 win over Germany in the final, with the Danes claiming the stunning victory without one of their greatest-ever players, following Michael Laudrup's decision to walk away from international football two years earlier to focus on his Barcelona career.

The mercurial midfielder had been central to the rise of Danish Dynamite, the thrilling side that reached the semi-finals of Euro 84 before winning over the hearts and minds of so many at the 1986 World Cup. But his decision to prioritise club football meant he would miss Denmark's greatest triumph.

Speaking about the Danish side of the 1980s, Laudrup credited his manager and his team-mates' decision to ply their trade in Europe's best leagues.

"A lot of the players were playing for big clubs in Europe, at a time when not many foreign players were allowed in European leagues," Laudrup tells FourFourTwo. "We had a lot of individual quality. The arrival of Sepp Piontek as manager in 1979 was also pivotal – he fulfilled our potential. We went to the European Championship and beat Yugoslavia 5-0. We had a fantastic game against Belgium too, which we won 3-2 from 2-0 down. In the end, we only lost on penalties in the semi-final against Spain.

"At the 1986 World Cup, we beat Uruguay 6-1 and West Germany 2-0, but then went out against Spain in the last 16. We were 1-0 up, but a poor second half cost us and we lost 5-1. The big countries had tournament experience. We learned from that and could apply it in 1992 and 1998, where we achieved good results in the latter stages."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

And what about his decision to quit the Denmark team in 1990?

"In the second game of qualifying, we drew in Northern Ireland, then we lost at home against Yugoslavia, who had a fantastic team," Laudrup continues. "I realised they’d qualify, even if we beat them away. I was also in the early stages of my time at Barça, which was important to me, and the two teams played completely different football. I wasn’t really happy with the way we played in the national team, but it’s always the manager’s decision. Still, I thought, ‘With this style of play, I can never be the same as at Barcelona.’

"As we weren’t able to qualify, I decided to focus 100 per cent on Barça. Yugoslavia went on to win the group, but because of the war, Denmark were suddenly given their place. People asked me if I wanted to go, but I didn’t want to join at the last moment, even though I could have. I felt it wouldn’t have been fair."

Laudrup would eventually return to the Danish national side in 1993.

"I’d won three league titles and the European Cup with Barça, and every time, they asked if I wanted to go back," he explains. "I’d achieved all the things I wanted with Barcelona, so I agreed. Unfortunately we lost a World Cup qualifier to Spain – the third time they got in our way, after beating us in 1984 and 1986. Spain has given me so much at personal and club level, then it’s curious how much it has taken away from me with the national team! But then we went to Euro 96 and the 1998 World Cup."

His 100th international cap came during the 1998 World Cup, with Laudrup calling time on his international career following their quarter-final defeat to Brazil.

"That was a great stage to retire on," he reflects. "After leaving Real Madrid, I went to Japan – I wanted to go somewhere I could still play, but also have a bit of freedom after being in Southern Europe since 1983. I thought maybe I should retire from the national team, but the coach asked me to continue. I realised that even though I liked life in Japan, I wanted to finish at a higher level. There was some interest from countries like Turkey and France – Marseille wanted me – but the Southern European passion was what I didn’t want any more! [Laughs]

"I joined Ajax – that team was incredible, with the De Boer brothers, Danny Blind, Edwin van der Sar and Jari Litmanen. We won the Double, so I continued with the national team, we qualified for the World Cup and lost in the quarter-finals to Brazil. We really challenged them and it was a great way to finish my career."

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#999. Chelsea star Cole Palmer escaped straight red card against Tottenham, says KMI panel

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Premier League's Key Match Incidents panel also identified missed decisions involving Aston Villa and Fulham, as it reviewed several contentious refereeing calls

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Chelsea forward Cole Palmer ought to have been dismissed ten minutes prior to his eventual sending-off against Tottenham, an independent assessment panel reviewing Premier League refereeing and VAR decisions has concluded.

Following an altercation between Palmer and Spurs player Mateus Fernandes during the 70th minute at Stamford Bridge on October 24, the Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel determined that the England international deserved a straight red card.

By a 3-2 majority, the five-member panel decided that referee Chris Kavanagh's initial call on the pitch was mistaken. Three panellists viewed Palmer's challenge on Fernandes as violent conduct warranting dismissal, noting there was "clear contact to the head" along with behaviour deemed "unnecessary, dangerous and made with excessive force".

Nevertheless, all five panellists agreed with VAR John Brooks's choice to refrain from advising an on-field review, backing his decision to stand by the original yellow card awarded by the match official.

Palmer was ultimately ordered off ten minutes later in the 80th minute after receiving a second booking following a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In a separate evaluation from the same day, the KMI panel judged that Aston Villa ought to have been awarded a spot-kick during their victory against Manchester City after Elliot Anderson tangled with Johan Manzambi.

Three members of the panel argued that Anderson made no effort to play the ball and intentionally widened his posture to block Manzambi's path.

Although a 3-2 majority felt the VAR was correct not to intervene with a review recommendation, two panel members contended that a clear and obvious error had occurred.

According to Premier League figures, 88 per cent of 162 key incidents evaluated by the panel this season were correctly judged on the pitch, matching performance levels from the same phase last year. That accuracy rate rises to 99 per cent once VAR intervention is taken into account.

Examining the fixture between Coventry and Fulham, the panel noted that VAR Jarred Gillett should have prompted referee Adam Herczeg to check a late first-half incident, despite agreeing with the ultimate outcome reached on the pitch and in the video room that no penalty be given to Fulham.

It noted an impactful hold by Fulham's Calvin Bassey prior to the corner kick being taken, succeeded by an infringement from Coventry's Bradley Thomas-Asante once the ball entered play. The panel accepted that the VAR had properly spotted both offences.

In its findings, the panel explained: "In this situation, as Bassey commits an offence before the ball is in play and the holding action of Thomas-Asante met the threshold for a penalty to be awarded, the VAR should recommend an on-field review to allow the referee to consider both holding actions and reach the correct outcome of retaken corner."

The Premier League is currently participating in an International Football Association Board trial that permits video officials to step in if an attacking player commits a pre-kick-off foul at set-pieces that directly affects a goal, penalty, or red-card decision.

#998. Gyokeres the creator and executioner to see nervous Arsenal past Slavia Prague

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal, but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is now growing in belief. Following this victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held on to long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.

Just as Gyokeres is finding his form, so is Madueke. The absence of the injured Bukayo Saka has given Madueke a run in the side and he seems to be benefiting from it, even if he still lacks the same consistency in decision-making as his England team-mate.

One of Slavia’s many problems in a one-sided first half was their inability to cope with Arsenal’s rotations in midfield. Declan Rice, Martín Zubimendi and Merino were all alternating positions at will, taking turns to drop deep and push forward. Merino could have scored a couple, before he combined sharply with Gyokeres for Arsenal’s second.

Gyokeres has never been the most delicate link-up player, and there have been too many times when the ball has simply bounced off him, but here he was impressively sleek. A quick exchange of passes with Merino allowed him a sight of goal, and the curled finish was sumptuous. For a man known for his power, this was an uncharacteristic demonstration of finesse.

Game over? Arsenal clearly thought so. They certainly came out for the second half like a team that believed the job was done. Arsenal’s critics will still grumble about the style of victory, but, of all clubs, this is a team who have no obligation to play in a way that neutrals might enjoy. Arsenal spent so much of Arsene Wenger’s 22-year reign playing football that was mostly stylish but only sometimes effective in big games. Now they are mostly effective but only occasionally stylish on such occasions. If you asked all the travelling fans at Anfield which they prefer, you would receive an overwhelming response.

David Raya has kept a clean sheet in 54% of his Champions League starts (21 clean sheets from 39 starts), the best ratio of any goalkeeper to start at least 25 games in the competition. 🤯🇪🇸 https://t.co/A1Zpn8kJN9

Arsenal return to Slavia Prague for the third time under Mikel Arteta knowing that three points will be another step towards a top-eight finish in the Champions League league phase.

Arteta’s team were 4-0 winners in the Czech capital in a 2021 Europa League quarter-final second leg, and 3-0 victors at this stage of the Champions League a year ago. Bukayo Saka opened the scoring with a penalty before two second-half goals from Mikel Merino.

Paris-St Germain are top of the table on 12 points after their rout against Villarreal last night. Real Madrid, Liverpool and Real Betis are the three teams who have the chance to join them on maximum points. Arsenal will jump to 10 points with a win, above Bayern Munich, Sporting and Aston Villa at a minimum.

Slavia Prague are top of the Czech league and unbeaten after 13 games this season, but they are winless in the Champions League after fixtures against Lens, Sabah and Fernerbahce.

The fixture should be a presentable opportunity for Arteta to rotate his team, especially after a physically taxing game at Anfield where Arsenal showed their mettle to win at Liverpool’s home for the first time since 2012.

Arsenal’s second-string is very strong, though they did not cover themselves in glory at Fleetwood in the League Cup last week when Max Dowman was sent off. Given the 16-year-old is banned for another two Premier League games, and the attention Arteta’s touchline reaction to the red card attracted, one wonders if he might want to seize a chance to put Dowman back on the horse.

William Saliba’s return to full training is very welcome news, despite Ezri Konsa impressing in his absence. Saliba travelled with the squad to Prague, and could make his first appearance of the season following a back injury which flared up in France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain. With fixtures against Manchester City, Borussia Dortmund, Brentford, Spurs, Real Madrid, Bournemouth and Manchester United before the end of 2026 though, they will not want rush him.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

#997. Goalkeeper involved in Jesus de Miguel death reveals ‘enormous pain’

Jesus Owono was sent off after colliding with De Miguel, who died in hospital on Tuesday after suffering a cardiac arrest

Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has said he feels “enormous pain” and is living through “the most difficult days of my life” following the death of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel.

De Miguel died in hospital on Tuesday following an accidental collision with Owono in stoppage time of the Spanish second division match between the teams on Monday.

Owono was sent off following the incident, which came as he came out of his box to clear the ball. The goalkeeper struck De Miguel in the chest at force, with the 30-year-old forward then suffering a cardiac arrest.

“These are the most difficult days of my life,” Owono, an Equatorial Guinea international, said in a statement released by his club Andorra on Wednesday. “I’m struggling to find the words and finding it very difficult to process anything that has happened.

“I feel enormous pain at the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and all the people who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I can’t think of anything other than Jesus and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesus.”

Tenerife announced six days of mourning following the death of De Miguel while tributes have flooded in from across the world of football. A minute’s silence was held before each of Tuesday night’s Champions League fixtures and will take place before all other Uefa fixtures this week.

Police on Tuesday confirmed they have opened a “routine” investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter, but criminal proceedings are unlikely. Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.

Owono deleted his Instagram account on Tuesday while Andorra defender Lautaro Spatz defended his team-mate.

“Those of us who know him know the type of person he is, how much he is suffering in these moments and that he would never intend to hurt anyone,” he said. “In football, unfortunate incidents happen, but no-one could imagine that one of these could end in such tragic circumstances.”

Fans gathered at Tenerife’s Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez stadium to lay tributes to De Miguel. A memorial service will be held at the ground on Saturday evening for the striker, with supporters invited to attend.

Barcelona’s Raphinha, who scored twice during their Champions League win over Aston Villa, paid tribute to De Miguel on Tuesday night, telling CBS Sports: “Today I don't want to talk about football, I want to send a message to the family of Jesus - may he rest in peace. From the club, I want to send a message of strength to the family.”

#996. Christian Pulisic and Folarin Balogun back on USMNT roster for Haiti clash

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Mauricio Pochettino unveiled his 25-man roster Wednesday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Balancing immediate competitive goals with long-term squad development, U.S. coach Mauricio Pochettino has recalled Christian Pulisic, Folarin Balogun, and Weston McKennie for the upcoming Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal against Haiti, alongside potential debutants Reed Baker-Whiting and Santiago Castañeda.

Unveiled on Wednesday, the 25-man selection features 19 players involved in September and October friendlies. The squad retains half of the 26 players from this year’s World Cup, including 10 starters from the tournament-ending defeat to Belgium, with six players under age 20.

"It’s very important for us to add more options, more players with the possibility to challenge the familiar faces," Pochettino said during an online news conference from London.

Pulisic returns after missing exhibition wins against Peru, Chile, Mexico, and Canada while recovering from a right tibia and fibula microfracture suffered in the 4-1 round-of-16 loss to Belgium at the World Cup.

Balogun, whose red-card suspension at the World Cup was controversially set aside following a phone call from U.S. President Donald Trump to Fifa head Gianni Infantino, was left out of those friendlies after sitting out Monaco's opening four Ligue 1 fixtures following a failed transfer to Everton. He has made five substitute appearances since.

"It’s a great opportunity to keep helping him to evolve after a tough summer, after the World Cup," Pochettino said.

The group's youngest contingent is led by striker Cavan Sullivan, who made his senior debut in September two days before turning 17 and became the youngest U.S. goalscorer a week later against Mexico. The roster also features 17-year-old midfielders Mathis Albert and Adri Mehmeti, 18-year-old forward Julian Hall, 19-year-old forward Justin Ellis, and 19-year-old defender Neil Pierre.

Baker-Whiting, a Nashville right back, and Castañeda, a Paderborn midfielder, are both 21.

Defender Bryan Reynolds, 25, earns his first call-up since the 2023 Concacaf Gold Cup after making his international debut at age 19 in 2021.

"They deserve the possibility to be with us, for us to feel them and for them to to see how they can fit in our national team," Pochettino said.

Players left out include goalkeeper Matt Turner, defenders Max Arfsten, Cameron Carter-Vickers, Mark McKenzie, and Joe Scally, midfielder Aidan Morris, and winger Tim Weah.

Following training in Georgia, the 16th-ranked Americans will play 84th-ranked Haiti on Nov. 14 in Miami and Nov. 17 in Cincinnati. The aggregate winner will secure a berth in the Nations League semifinals scheduled for March 22-30 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Players dropped from the September squad include goalkeeper Chris Brady, defenders Miles Robinson and Frankie Westfield, midfielders Zavier Gozo and Yunus Musah, and forwards Cole Campbell and Damion Downs.

Several unselected players will join the under-23 team preparing for the 2028 Olympic Games, with that training camp roster set to be announced Thursday.

Injuries ruled out defender Miles Robinson, midfielder Johnny Cardoso, and forwards Haji Wright and Alejandro Zendejas. Striker Ricardo Pepi was also left off following a leg muscle injury that kept him out from Sept. 20 until last Saturday.

Defender George Campbell was selected but left West Bromwich Albion's match on Tuesday due to an injury and could be replaced.

Goalkeepers: Matt Freese (New York City), Diego Kochen (Lyngby), Brian Schwake (Nashville).

Defenders: Reed Baker-Whiting (Nashville), George Campbell (West Bromwich Albion), Sergiño Dest (PSV Eindhoven), Alex Freeman (Villarreal), Neil Pierre (Philadelphia), Bryan Reynolds (Rennes), Chris Richards (Crystal Palace), Antonee Robinson (Fulham), Auston Trusty (Celtic).

Midfielders: Tyler Adams (Bournemouth), Mathis Albert (Borussia Dortmund), Sebastian Berhalter (Middlesbrough), Santiago Castañeda (Paderborn), Weston McKennie (Juventus), Adri Mehmeti (New York Red Bulls), Gio Reyna (Strasbourg), Malik Tillman (Bayer Leverkusen).

Forwards: Folarin Balogun (Monaco), Justin Ellis (Orlando), Julian Hall (New York Red Bulls), Christian Pulisic (AC Milan), Cavan Sullivan (Philadelphia).
